heuristics.rule: If your departure date is mid-year and your income is low in that partial year, withdraw from RRSP before leaving rather than after
heuristics.condition: When you are leaving Canada partway through a calendar year and your total Canadian income for that year will be below normal...
heuristics.action: ...make RRSP withdrawals before your departure date to be taxed at a lower marginal rate instead of the flat 25% non-resident withholding rate
heuristics.because: Once you become a non-resident, every RRSP withdrawal is subject to flat 25% withholding (no treaty reduction for India or China); partial-year Canadian income may put you in a lower marginal bracket, making pre-departure withdrawal cheaper

heuristics.rule: Stop all TFSA contributions on the exact date you leave Canada — not the end of the year
heuristics.condition: When you are departing Canada and becoming a non-resident for tax purposes...
heuristics.action: ...cease TFSA contributions immediately on departure date and do not contribute afterward
heuristics.because: Any TFSA contribution made while a non-resident triggers a 1% per month penalty on that amount; the penalty compounds monthly and is easy to accidentally incur if you have automatic contributions set up

heuristics.rule: If you own Canadian real estate and plan to sell, sell before departure rather than as a non-resident
heuristics.condition: When you anticipate selling Canadian property within a few years of leaving...
heuristics.action: ...either sell before departing or budget explicitly for the buyer withholding 25% of the gross sale price (not profit) for months during clearance certificate processing
heuristics.because: The Section 116 withholding is on the full sale price — not the gain — creating a massive temporary cash flow gap; a $800K sale means $200K held by the buyer, which can take months to recover even if your actual tax bill is far lower

heuristics.rule: Do not over-contribute to RRSP in your final Canadian years if you plan to leave
heuristics.condition: When you know or suspect you will be leaving Canada within 1–3 years...
heuristics.action: ...limit RRSP contributions to amounts you can realistically draw down at favorable rates before departure or accept will be subject to 25% flat non-resident withholding indefinitely
heuristics.because: RRSP withdrawals as a non-resident from India or China face 25% withholding with no treaty reduction, meaning excess RRSP balances become a tax-inefficient asset compared to non-registered accounts where you have more exit flexibility

heuristics.rule: Maintain your Social Insurance Number records even after leaving Canada
heuristics.condition: When you have contributed to CPP over your Canadian working years...
heuristics.action: ...keep your SIN documented securely so you can eventually claim your CPP retirement pension from abroad
heuristics.because: CPP entitlements survive departure and can be paid to a foreign bank account, but the claim process requires your SIN; losing it creates bureaucratic barriers to recovering money you already contributed

decision_factors.factor: RRSP balance and treaty withholding rate
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The applicable non-resident withholding rate on RRSP withdrawals determines whether leaving RRSP funds in Canada is efficient; India and China get no treaty reduction, meaning 25% is the permanent rate on every future withdrawal
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check your home country's tax treaty with Canada specifically for pension/RRSP withholding rates; calculate your total RRSP balance and model the after-tax value under 25% withholding versus alternatives

decision_factors.factor: Non-registered investment portfolio size and unrealized gains
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Departure tax (deemed disposition) is triggered on non-registered investments at the moment you leave; larger portfolios with larger unrealized gains create larger immediate tax bills
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate current fair market value minus adjusted cost base for all non-registered holdings; estimate the capital gains tax at 50% inclusion rate at your expected marginal rate in the departure year

decision_factors.factor: Departure date timing within the calendar year
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Leaving mid-year reduces your Canadian income for that year, potentially lowering your marginal rate for both RRSP withdrawals and deemed disposition gains — creating a planning window
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Project total Canadian income from January to departure date; model RRSP withdrawal scenarios at that lower income level versus the flat 25% non-resident rate post-departure

decision_factors.factor: Canadian real estate ownership and intended sale timeline
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Selling Canadian real estate as a non-resident triggers Section 116 withholding at 25% of gross sale price — creating a major cash flow problem even when actual tax owed is far less
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether you plan to sell within a few years of departure; if yes, compare the net proceeds and process complexity of selling before versus after becoming a non-resident

decision_factors.factor: Strength of Canadian residential ties being severed
decision_factors.why_it_matters: If you fail to sever primary ties (home, spouse, dependents in Canada), CRA may continue to treat you as a Canadian tax resident even while you live abroad, resulting in ongoing worldwide taxation
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Audit all primary and secondary residential ties using CRA's framework; document evidence of tie severance (lease termination, spouse relocation, cancellation of provincial health card, driver's license, etc.)

decision_factors.why_it_matters: If you withdrew from RRSP under the Home Buyers' Plan or Lifelong Learning Plan, the repayment obligation continues post-departure; failure to repay adds the required repayment amount to your income each year
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check your CRA My Account for outstanding HBP/LLP repayment balances and annual repayment schedule; calculate the cost of not repaying versus repaying before departure

decision_factors.why_it_matters: CPP entitlements are preserved after leaving Canada and represent a future income stream from your Canadian working years; they should factor into retirement income planning
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Review CPP Statement of Contributions through Service Canada; estimate projected CPP pension at age 65 based on years and amounts contributed

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Leaving RRSP funds in Canada and withdrawing gradually as a non-resident
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Every withdrawal is permanently subject to 25% flat withholding for residents of India or China, with no treaty reduction — meaning a $100,000 RRSP is effectively worth only $75,000 net, with no ability to optimize timing or bracket
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Indian and Chinese nationals who accumulate large RRSPs expecting tax-deferred growth to compound efficiently for retirement

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Maintaining any Canadian residential tie while working abroad (renting out your home, leaving spouse in Canada)
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: CRA may classify you as a continuing Canadian tax resident, subjecting your global income — including your new home country salary — to Canadian income tax
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Professionals who try to 'keep options open' by maintaining Canadian ties while testing opportunities abroad

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Selling Canadian real estate as a non-resident rather than before departure
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The buyer is legally required to withhold 25% of the gross sale price — not the profit — creating a months-long cash flow gap while the Section 116 clearance certificate is processed; on a $800K sale, $200K is locked up with the buyer
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Non-residents who are counting on sale proceeds to fund resettlement or investment in their home country and did not anticipate the withholding delay

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Continuing to contribute to TFSA after departure date without canceling automatic contributions
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Each month of non-resident TFSA contribution triggers a 1% penalty on the contributed amount — an easily avoidable cost that compounds until discovered and corrected
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Professionals who set up automatic TFSA contributions and forget to cancel them when departing

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Ignoring the departure tax and assuming Canada stops taxing you the moment you leave
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A deemed disposition triggers on all non-registered investments on departure date, creating a capital gains tax bill in the departure year even though no actual sale occurred and no cash was received
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Passive investors with large non-registered portfolios who built wealth in Canada but planned to simply 'walk away' without triggering a tax event

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Not filing a departure return or notifying CRA of non-resident status
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Canadian employers or financial institutions may continue reporting income and withholding on the assumption you are still a resident, creating administrative and reconciliation problems that are difficult to unwind from abroad
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Professionals who leave informally without a clean administrative departure from Canadian tax obligations

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating RRSP like a 401k and assuming it can be efficiently accessed after leaving Canada
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The RRSP-401k analogy is commonly used; professionals assume similar favorable withdrawal treatment, not knowing that Canada's treaties with India and China provide zero withholding reduction unlike some US treaty provisions
failure_patterns.consequence: Permanent 25% tax drag on every RRSP withdrawal for life, with no optimization possible after becoming a non-resident — reducing the effective value of accumulated RRSP savings by 25%
warning_signs: Maximizing RRSP contributions in final years before departure without modeling the non-resident withdrawal cost
Assuming RRSP will behave like a tax-advantaged account in retirement from abroad

failure_patterns.pattern: Underestimating the cash flow impact of Section 116 withholding when selling Canadian real estate as a non-resident
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Sellers focus on the capital gain calculation (profit) and estimate their tax correctly, but do not realize the withholding is applied to gross sale price — creating a much larger temporary cash lockup than the actual tax owed
failure_patterns.consequence: Months of illiquidity with hundreds of thousands of dollars held by the buyer, disrupting resettlement plans or forcing reliance on other funds during the clearance certificate delay
warning_signs: Planning to use real estate sale proceeds immediately after closing to fund home purchase or investment in home country
Not budgeting for a 3–6 month delay between sale closing and receipt of withheld funds

failure_patterns.pattern: Failing to sever Canadian residential ties cleanly, triggering continued Canadian tax residency while abroad
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Professionals want optionality — they rent out their condo, leave a spouse behind temporarily, or keep provincial health coverage 'just in case' — without realizing each tie individually or collectively may cause CRA to classify them as continuing residents
failure_patterns.consequence: Continued obligation to report worldwide income to Canada and pay Canadian tax on foreign salary, creating double taxation risk and compliance burden
warning_signs: Renting out Canadian home while working abroad rather than selling or terminating lease
Maintaining provincial health insurance card after departure date

failure_patterns.pattern: Not planning RRSP withdrawals around departure date timing
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Professionals focus on logistics of moving and career transition; tax timing optimization feels like a secondary concern and is often deferred until after the move when it is too late
failure_patterns.consequence: Missing the window to withdraw RRSP funds at a lower marginal rate during a partial departure year, instead facing the permanent 25% flat non-resident withholding rate on all future withdrawals
warning_signs: Departure planned for mid-year with RRSP balance untouched and no withdrawal strategy in place
Engaging a tax advisor only after the departure date has passed

failure_patterns.pattern: Forgetting HBP or LLP repayment obligations after leaving Canada
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The repayment obligation is abstract — there is no invoice or collection agency; professionals simply stop thinking about it once they leave Canada and stop filing regular Canadian returns
failure_patterns.consequence: The outstanding HBP/LLP balance is added to taxable income each year the repayment is missed, creating unexpected Canadian tax liabilities that may only surface during a future tax audit or when applying for Canadian financial products
warning_signs: Previously used RRSP Home Buyers' Plan or Lifelong Learning Plan and has not confirmed the repayment schedule
Assuming that leaving Canada ends all RRSP-related obligations

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your current RRSP balance, and do you know your home country's non-resident withholding rate under the Canada tax treaty?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines the actual after-tax value of your RRSP as a non-resident and whether pre-departure withdrawal strategies should be pursued
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Model the partial-year marginal rate scenario: is your effective rate in the departure year lower than 25%? If so, quantify how much to withdraw before leaving.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Look up the Canada tax treaty with your home country specifically for the pension/RRSP article — do not assume any reduction exists; India and China receive no reduction from the default 25%

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you planning to sell your Canadian property before or after you leave, and do you know what Section 116 withholding means for your cash flow?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the person has modeled the gross-price withholding versus the gain-based tax bill, and whether they have budgeted for months of illiquidity
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask for their timeline: when do they need the proceeds? If within 6 months of closing, the clearance certificate delay could be a serious problem.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Walk through the mechanics: 25% of gross sale price is withheld by the buyer, not 25% of gain — on an $800K property, that is $200K held up regardless of actual tax owed

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you severed — or do you plan to sever — all primary Canadian residential ties before your intended departure date?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Identifies whether the person is at risk of being classified as a continuing Canadian tax resident despite physically living abroad
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask specifically about the home (sold or lease terminated?), spouse and dependents (relocating with you?), and provincial health card (cancelled?).
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Explain the 'extended stay overseas' trap: CRA does not automatically reclassify you as a non-resident; maintaining a home or spouse in Canada is sufficient to sustain Canadian tax residency

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your planned departure date, and have you modeled your total Canadian income for that partial calendar year?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether there is a planning window to make RRSP withdrawals or realize non-registered gains at a lower marginal rate before departure
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Run the numbers: what is the effective marginal rate on incremental income in that partial year? Compare to the flat 25% RRSP withholding rate post-departure.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The departure date is one of the most important tax planning variables — even a few months of difference changes whether pre-departure RRSP withdrawal is advantageous

diagnostic_questions.question: Did you use the RRSP Home Buyers' Plan or Lifelong Learning Plan, and do you know your outstanding repayment balance?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Identifies a silent ongoing obligation that continues post-departure and can generate unexpected Canadian taxable income if ignored
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Calculate the annual repayment amount and decide whether to repay the full balance before departure (using current marginal rate) or accept the annual income inclusion going forward.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Check CRA My Account for HBP/LLP balances before finalizing departure plans — this is frequently overlooked and creates avoidable tax exposure

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a non-registered investment portfolio in Canada, and have you calculated your adjusted cost base on those holdings?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines the size of the deemed disposition tax hit on departure and whether pre-departure realization of gains (when Canadian marginal rates may be lower) is preferable to the deemed disposition
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Compare tax cost of realizing gains before departure at partial-year marginal rate versus deemed disposition at the same rate — they may be equivalent, but timing of actual cash payment differs.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Many investors do not track ACB carefully; without it, calculating the departure tax obligation is impossible and CRA may use a conservative (unfavorable) estimate

industry_realities.common_belief: Once you leave Canada and stop living there, Canada stops taxing you automatically
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canada uses a residential ties test, not a physical presence count; if you maintain a home, spouse, or dependents in Canada, CRA may continue to classify you as a Canadian resident for tax purposes regardless of where you physically live
industry_realities.implication: You must actively sever primary residential ties and document that severance — departure alone is insufficient; professionals who maintain optionality by keeping Canadian ties face continued worldwide tax obligations

industry_realities.common_belief: RRSP is like a 401k and will be similarly efficient to access from abroad
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canada's tax treaties with India and China provide no reduction in the 25% default withholding rate on RRSP withdrawals; unlike some US treaty provisions that reduce pension withholding, every dollar withdrawn from an RRSP as a non-resident in these countries is taxed at 25% flat
industry_realities.implication: Professionals from India or China should model RRSP as a 75-cents-on-the-dollar asset in retirement — and weigh whether pre-departure withdrawals at a lower marginal rate are more efficient than leaving funds for future non-resident withdrawals

industry_realities.common_belief: Selling your Canadian home as a non-resident is similar to selling it as a resident — you pay tax on the gain
industry_realities.actual_reality: The buyer is legally required to withhold 25% of the gross sale price — not the gain — as a security deposit under Section 116; on a $700K–$900K property, this locks up $175K–$225K for months while a clearance certificate is processed
industry_realities.implication: Cash flow planning must account for the withholding delay, not just the tax bill; professionals expecting to access sale proceeds quickly for resettlement or reinvestment will face a significant liquidity gap

industry_realities.common_belief: TFSA is a simple, penalty-free account that you can manage from anywhere
industry_realities.actual_reality: Any TFSA contribution made while you are a non-resident triggers a 1% per month penalty on the contributed amount; contribution room also stops accumulating while you are a non-resident
industry_realities.implication: Automatic TFSA contributions must be canceled on the departure date — not at year end — and you should not assume TFSA room keeps growing while you are abroad

industry_realities.common_belief: There is no Canadian exit tax equivalent to the US exit tax
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canada has a deemed disposition rule that treats you as having sold all non-registered investments at fair market value on the day you leave; this triggers capital gains tax on unrealized appreciation even though you have not actually sold anything
industry_realities.implication: Professionals with large non-registered portfolios must calculate and plan for this departure tax bill before leaving — it is real cash owed on paper gains, and it comes due on the final Canadian tax return

industry_realities.common_belief: You need to formally notify CRA when you leave Canada
industry_realities.actual_reality: There is no mandatory notification form — you simply include your departure date on your final tax return; however, without proactive communication, Canadian employers and financial institutions may continue treating you as a resident, causing withholding and reporting problems
industry_realities.implication: Consider filing a letter to CRA clarifying non-resident status to prevent institutions from continuing to report Canadian income incorrectly and to establish a clean administrative departure date

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Maximizes RRSP contributions in final Canadian years because 'tax deduction now is always good' without modeling what withdrawal looks like as a non-resident from a country with no treaty reduction
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Models the full lifecycle: contribution deduction value now versus the flat 25% non-resident withholding on every withdrawal later; may deliberately under-contribute or do partial pre-departure withdrawals at lower marginal rates
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The RRSP tax deferral benefit reverses if the exit withholding rate exceeds the original marginal rate benefit; optimizing contributions without modeling the exit creates a worse outcome than not contributing at all

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Focuses on the capital gain calculation and estimated tax, concluding 'I know what I'll owe' — without realizing the withholding is on gross sale price and creates a multi-month cash flow disruption
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Plans the real estate exit as part of the departure timeline, models the $200K+ cash flow gap from Section 116 withholding, and either sells before departure or arranges bridge financing to cover the withholding period
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A technically correct tax estimate can coexist with a completely incorrect cash flow plan — the distinction between tax owed and cash withheld is the difference between a smooth transition and a liquidity crisis

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes that physically moving to another country ends Canadian tax obligations; may keep a rented-out condo, maintain provincial health coverage, or leave a spouse in Canada temporarily while 'trying out' the home country
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats tie severance as a deliberate legal act requiring documentation; proactively cancels provincial health coverage, terminates leases, relocates family together, and documents the departure date clearly to establish non-resident status
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Maintaining even primary residential ties while abroad can result in CRA treating global income as taxable in Canada — creating double taxation and compliance exposure that is difficult to unwind retroactively

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Believes departure tax does not apply to Canada because 'Canada is not like the US' and assumes no exit tax consequences on non-registered investments
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Knows Canada's deemed disposition rule creates a capital gains event on departure for non-registered holdings; calculates the departure tax ahead of time and times the departure date to minimize the marginal rate applied to those gains
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: An unplanned departure tax bill on a large non-registered portfolio can be $10,000–$50,000+ — discovered only when filing the final return, with no remaining ability to optimize

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Does not think about HBP or LLP repayment after leaving Canada because 'I'm not filing Canadian taxes anymore so it doesn't matter'
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Checks outstanding HBP/LLP balance before departure, calculates the annual income inclusion cost of not repaying, and makes a deliberate decision whether to repay the full balance pre-departure or accept the ongoing inclusion
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Ignoring HBP/LLP repayment generates unexpected Canadian taxable income each year — creating ongoing filing obligations and tax bills that were entirely avoidable with pre-departure planning
